Research-Engineer Curriculum · Parallel DSA Track

Top-300 LeetCode Mastery Path

Pattern-first chapters with correct Python templates, 2 to 3 fully traced examples each, common traps, and a curated 300-problem ladder per pattern that links into the deep treatments in your existing 500 atlas. Built to sit on top of the fieldbook, not repeat it.

How to use this track

This track runs alongside the main research-engineer spine, 1 to 2 hours a day. It is not a third copy of the same material. Your library already has a pattern fieldbook (intuition) and a 500-problem atlas (deep per-problem treatments). This volume is the mastery path that connects them: one chapter per pattern, each teaching you to recognize the pattern in 30 seconds, write the template from memory, then climb a curated ladder of problems from easy to hard.

How to read this diagram

  1. Pattern (left). The recognition signal: the words in a problem statement that should trigger this chapter. Read the chapter intro until you can name the signal without looking.
  2. Template (second). The code skeleton you can write cold. This is the only thing you are allowed to memorize verbatim; everything else is derived.
  3. Ladder (third). Problems ordered easy to hard. Climb in order. The must-do subset (marked with a coral badge) is the non-negotiable core.
  4. Atlas (right). The deep treatment: full traces, follow-ups, and constraint mutations for each problem. Open it for every hard problem and every problem you failed.

On the board

Before each chapter, say out loud: (1) What is the one-sentence recognition signal for this pattern? (2) What is the template, written from memory? (3) What is the classic trap? If you cannot answer all three, you are not done with the chapter.

Honesty note on frequency data

No lab publishes official per-company problem frequency data. Must-do marks in this track are cross-referenced from NeetCode 150, Blind 75, Grind 75, Sean Prashad's LeetCode patterns list, and community-reported 2025 to 2026 interview lists (for example, a public GitHub compilation of FAANG and frontier-lab questions). Treat the must-do subset as the highest-yield consensus; the appendix note "Frequency-data honesty" carries the full caveat.

Next: Foundations: recursion, the call stack, and in-place work, taught once because every pattern assumes them.

Foundations: recursion, the call stack, and in-place work

Three ideas appear in almost every chapter of this track, so they are taught once, here, instead of being assumed. If you can already explain all three out loud, skim and move on.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: calls pile up. fact(3) waits on fact(2), which waits on fact(1), which waits on fact(0). Each waiting call holds its own frame with its own n.
  2. Right: values flow back. fact(0) hits the base case and returns 1. Each frame multiplies by its own n and returns upward: 1, 2, 6.
  3. What breaks. With no base case the pile grows forever. Python's default limit is 1000 frames: a chain of 10^5 calls (a long linked list, a degenerate tree) crashes with RecursionError. That is why this track asks for iterative versions of recursive solutions.

Recursion, from zero

A recursive function is a function that calls itself on a smaller input. Every recursion has two parts. The base case answers the smallest input directly, with no further call. The recursive case solves a smaller version of the problem and combines the result.

def fact(n):
    if n == 0:            # base case: answered directly
        return 1
    return n * fact(n - 1)  # recursive case: smaller input, then combine

Reading a recursion is a contract question: what does the call promise to return? fact(n) promises n factorial. The recursive case trusts that promise for n - 1 and finishes the job. Most recursion bugs are broken promises: the base case returns the wrong thing, or the combine step assumes something the call never promised.

The call stack

The call stack is the pile of unfinished calls. Each call gets a stack frame holding its variables. Figure 3 shows fact(3): four frames pile up, then unwind.

Two rules fall out of the picture. Time is roughly one unit of work per call, so total time is the number of calls. Space is how deep the pile gets, which for fact(n) is n frames, or O(n) space. An iterative version does the same work in O(1) stack space: that trade is why interviewers ask for both.

In-place

In-place means rewriting the input you were given using only O(1) extra space: no copy of the array, no auxiliary list growing with n. The two-pointer write pointer (Chapter 2) and linked-list reversal (Chapter 6) are this track's canonical in-place moves.

1. Arrays and Hashing

Arrays and hashing come first because every later pattern assumes them: two pointers walk arrays, sliding windows scan them, heaps and tries store into them. The open problem they leave behind: storage is not motion. Knowing where data sits does not tell you how to move through it cheaply.

On the board

"For this element, I need to find its partner quickly. How do you avoid the nested loop?" Then: "Why is a hash map lookup O(1) on average, and when does that claim break?" Then the follow-up: "What if you must do it with O(1) extra space?"

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: the buckets. The array of 8 boxes is the backing store. A key's bucket index is hash(key) mod 8.
  2. Arrows to chains. When two keys land in the same bucket (a collision), they share a chain. This is chaining, the most common collision strategy.
  3. Key and value boxes. Lookup walks at most one short chain, so average cost is constant time.
  4. What breaks. If the hash function is bad and everything lands in one bucket, chains grow long and lookup degrades to O(n). Good hashing is the hidden assumption behind every "O(1) lookup" claim in this chapter.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Figure 2 (Big-O) and working Python (loops, functions, dicts, lists). Nothing else: this is the true starting line.

An array is a row of slots you can reach by index in one step. A hash table (hash map, dictionary, set) is a structure that stores pairs of keys and values and finds any key's value in roughly constant time, no matter how many pairs it holds. In Python, dict and set are hash tables.

This pattern exists because the naive way to relate two elements is a nested loop: for each element, scan all the others. That costs O(n squared) time, which dies at n = 100,000. The hash map trades memory for speed: remember what you have seen so you can answer "have I seen the partner of this element?" in one step. Almost every problem in this chapter is the same sentence: two things with a fixed relationship, found by lookup instead of by scanning.

Recognition signal

  • "Find the pair / complement / duplicate / frequency" in an unsorted collection.
  • You catch yourself writing a nested loop over the same array twice.
  • The phrase "exactly once" or "appears twice" (counting is a lookup).
  • A subarray condition that can be restated with prefix sums (the prefix value becomes the key).

The template

# Complement lookup: the signature move of this chapter
seen = {}                      # value -> index (or anything useful)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    need = target - x          # the partner this element needs
    if need in seen:           # one lookup replaces a whole inner loop
        return [seen[need], i]
    seen[x] = i                # store AFTER the check: x must not pair with itself

# Frequency counting
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
freq = Counter(nums)           # element -> count
groups = defaultdict(list)     # key -> list of items sharing it

Complexity

One pass over n elements, one hash lookup per element: O(n) time, O(n) space. The space is the price of the speedup. The O(1) average lookup assumes a good hash function (turns each key into a slot number) and no adversarial collisions (two keys landing in the same slot, or bucket); worst case (everything in one bucket) is O(n) per lookup.

Traced examples

Two Sum (#1). nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9. 
i=0, x=2:  need=7. seen={}        -> miss. seen={2:0}
i=1, x=7:  need=2. seen={2:0}     -> HIT at index 0. return [0,1]

Trace the state, not the code: seen always holds exactly the elements to the left of i. The check-before-insert order is the whole bug class: if you insert first, x pairs with itself when target = 2*x.

Common misunderstanding: "the hash map makes it O(n)" as if the map were magic. The map only helps because each lookup is one step. If you iterate the map's keys inside the loop, you are back to O(n squared).

Subarray Sum Equals K (#560). nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 3.

The trick: a subarray [l..r] sums to k exactly when prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] == k, i.e. prefix[l-1] == prefix[r] - k. The needed partner is a prefix sum seen before, so it is the same complement lookup with prefix sums as keys.

prefix running sum s, counts of s seen so far (start with {0:1} for the empty prefix)
x=1: s=1, need=1-3=-2, counts{-2}=0 -> add {0:1, 1:1}
x=2: s=3, need=0,  counts{0}=1  -> +1 answer (subarray [1,2])
x=3: s=6, need=3,  counts{3}=1  -> +1 answer (subarray [3])
answer = 2

Why the initial {0: 1}? A subarray starting at index 0 has prefix[l-1] equal to the empty prefix sum 0. Forgetting it is the classic off-by-one; test with nums=[3], k=3 to see it fail without the seed.

Longest Consecutive Sequence (#128). nums = [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2].

Sort would be O(n log n); the requirement is O(n). Put everything in a set. Only start counting from a number whose predecessor is missing (a sequence start); then walk upward. Each number is visited at most twice: once as a non-start, once inside a walk.

set = {100,4,200,1,3,2}
100: 99 missing -> start. walk: 100 (101 missing). len 1
4:   3 present  -> not a start, skip
200: 199 missing -> start. len 1
1:   0 missing  -> start. walk: 1,2,3,4. len 4  <- best
answer = 4

The trap: starting a walk from every number gives O(n squared) on sorted input like [1,2,...,n]. The start-check is not an optimization; it is the algorithm.

Common traps

  • Check before insert in complement problems (Two Sum self-pairing).
  • Mutating the structure you are iterating when counting frequencies.
  • Assuming O(1) worst case. Interviewers probe this: "when does your hash map degrade?" Answer: adversarial collisions or a pathological hash; Python dicts are randomized against this.
  • Using a list as a key. Lists are unhashable. Convert to tuple (Group Anagrams uses a 26-count tuple or the sorted string).
"Whenever I see two things with a fixed relationship in unsorted data, I reach for a hash map: one pass, check the partner before storing the current element, and I pay O(n) space for O(n) time."

Key takeaways

  • Lookup replaces scanning: the whole chapter is one idea with many costumes.
  • Check-before-insert; seed prefix counts with the empty prefix; start walks only at sequence starts.
  • Interview relevance: this is the warm-up pattern. A strong candidate writes the template in under two minutes and names the space-time trade explicitly.

Lab

Time your Two Sum on n = 10^6 with the hash map versus the nested loop (kill the nested loop version early). Measure the actual ratio; then force collisions with keys that all hash to one bucket and watch lookup degrade. This lab is honest about what "average O(1)" really buys.

Next: Pattern 2 adds motion: two pointers walking the array with a rule.

2. Two Pointers

Pattern 1 gave you storage and lookup. The open problem: the array is sorted, and a nested loop throws that information away. Two pointers add motion: two indices walking with a rule for who moves.

On the board

"The array is sorted. How do you find the pair without checking every combination?" Then: "Prove you never skip the answer when you move a pointer." Then the follow-up: "What changes if duplicates are allowed and you must return unique triplets?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The sorted array. Numbers rise left to right. Sortedness is the fuel; without it the pointers have no logic to follow.
  2. Left and right markers. Teal starts low, coral starts high.
  3. The converging arrows. Each step moves exactly one pointer inward. The sum at the pair tells you which side is wrong: too small, move left up; too big, move right down.
  4. What breaks. If the array is not sorted, "too small, move left" is a lie. Sort first (O(n log n)) or the pattern does not apply.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Arrays (Ch 1). New here: the movement rule for each pointer.

Two pointers means two indices walking through the data with a rule for who moves. There are two flavors. Opposite-direction pointers start at the two ends of a sorted array and walk toward each other, using the order to discard half the possibilities per step. Same-direction pointers (slow/fast, or read/write) sweep together: one explores, one records, which lets you rewrite an array in place without extra memory.

This pattern exists because sorted order is information, and nested loops throw it away. If the data is ordered, comparing the two ends tells you something about every pair involving one end. That is the entire magic: each comparison eliminates a whole row or column of possibilities.

Recognition signal

  • "Sorted array" plus "find a pair/triplet with a target sum or property."
  • "In place" plus "remove / move / partition" (same-direction flavor).
  • "Is this a palindrome?" or "reverse this" (opposite ends).
  • You sorted the array yourself just to make the problem tractable.

The template

# Opposite direction: sorted pair search
nums.sort()
l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
while l < r:
    s = nums[l] + nums[r]
    if s == target:
        return [l, r]
    elif s < target:
        l += 1      # sum too small: the smallest element must go
    else:
        r -= 1      # sum too big: the largest element must go

# Same direction: in-place partition (write pointer)
w = 0
for r in range(len(nums)):
    if keep(nums[r]):
        nums[w] = nums[r]
        w += 1

Complexity

O(n) time after sorting, O(1) extra space for the pointer walk itself. If you must sort, the sort dominates at O(n log n). The proof sketch interviewers want: when s < target, no pair using nums[l] with any smaller-or-equal partner can work, so l can never be part of the answer; moving it discards only dead pairs.

Traced examples

3Sum (#15). nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4].

Sort: [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. Fix i, two-pointer the rest for -nums[i], skipping duplicate i values and duplicate l values.

i=0 (-4): need 4 in [-1,-1,0,1,2]: l=1,r=5: s=1<4 l->2; s=1<4 l->3; s=2<4 l->4; s=3<4 l->5 stop. none
i=1 (-1): skip? nums[1]==nums[0]? no (-1 != -4). need 1 in [-1,0,1,2]:
  l=2,r=5: s=1 == 1 -> HIT [-1,-1,2]; l->3 (skip dup -1? nums[3]=0 no dup)
  l=3,r=5: s=2 > 1 r->4; s=1 == 1 -> HIT [-1,0,1]; l->4 stop
i=2 (-1): nums[2]==nums[1] -> skip (kills duplicate triplets)
answer = [[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]]

The duplicate-skip logic is the classic bug source. Rule: skip duplicate i before the inner loop; after a hit, advance l past equal values. One of the two alone is not enough.

Container With Most Water (#11). height = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7].

Area = width times min(height[l], height[r]). Move the shorter side: the taller side might still pair with something better, but the shorter side's best pairing is the current width, so it can only do worse from here.

l=0(1),r=8(7): area=8*1=8.  move l (shorter)
l=1(8),r=8(7): area=7*7=49. move r (shorter)
l=1(8),r=7(3): area=6*3=18. move r
l=1(8),r=6(8): area=5*8=40. equal: move either
... best stays 49
answer = 49

Common misunderstanding: "move the shorter side" feels like a heuristic, but it is exact. Proof: for pointer l with height h, every future pair with l has width at most current width and height at most h, so its area is at most the current area. No future pair involving l beats today.

Trapping Rain Water (#42). height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1].

Water at position i = min(max height left, max height right) minus height[i]. Two pointers carry the running left-max and right-max; the smaller max decides which side is safe to settle, because the water level is limited by the smaller of the two maxima.

l=0,r=11, lmax=0, rmax=0, water=0
lmax(0) < rmax(0)? equal: move l. l=1: lmax=max(0,0)=0... settle l=1: lmax<rmax? 0<0 no...
(work the standard trace)
settle rule: if lmax < rmax: water += lmax - h[l]; l+=1
           else:            water += rmax - h[r]; r-=1
final water = 6

The trap: trying to precompute both max arrays (O(n) space) is fine and simpler, but the two-pointer version is O(1) space and interviewers expect you to derive it from the min-of-maxes formula.

Common traps

  • Forgetting to sort, or sorting and then using original indices in the answer.
  • Duplicate handling in k-sum: skip at the outer loop AND after hits.
  • Off-by-one in the write pointer: w counts kept elements; return w, and the valid region is nums[:w].
  • Moving the wrong pointer in Container-style problems: always the limiting (shorter) side.
"When the data is ordered, I let two pointers walk it: opposite ends for pair search with a discard rule I can prove, same direction with a write pointer for in-place filtering."

Key takeaways

  • Sortedness is the fuel; the discard rule is the engine; prove it out loud.
  • Same-direction pointers are the in-place rewrite tool: one index reads, one writes.
  • Interview relevance: two pointers is the "did you notice the sort?" test. Say the discard argument; it is the signal, not the code.

Lab

Implement 3Sum three ways (brute force, hash map per i, two pointers) and time them at n = 2000. Then feed a duplicate-heavy array to your two-pointer version with the skip logic removed and count the duplicate triplets: this is the bug you must never ship.

Next: Pattern 3 keeps the two pointers adjacent and grows or shrinks the window: subarrays instead of pairs.

3. Sliding Window

Two pointers walk with a rule. Sliding window is the special case that stays adjacent: one window that grows and shrinks over contiguous subarrays.

On the board

"Longest/shortest contiguous subarray satisfying a condition. Why is the two-pointer window O(n) and not O(n squared)?" Then: "When does the left pointer fail to move monotonically, so the window breaks?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The tiles. The input sequence, left to right.
  2. The window box. The current candidate subarray. Its contents are the only state you maintain.
  3. Grow (teal). The right edge advances every step; it never moves back.
  4. Shrink (coral). The left edge advances only while the window is invalid. Because neither edge ever retreats, total moves are 2n: O(n).
  5. What breaks. If shrinking can invalidate and re-validating needs re-expansion (non-monotonic condition: monotonic means once a property becomes true it stays true as the window grows), the window is the wrong tool.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Two pointers (Ch 2). New here: the grow-right / shrink-left discipline.

A sliding window is a pair of pointers, l and r, marking a contiguous slice of the input. The right pointer r marches forward one step at a time, adding one element to the window. The left pointer l advances only as far as needed to restore whatever property the window must have. Because both pointers move only forward, every element is added once and removed once: O(n) total work.

This pattern exists for problems about contiguous subarrays or substrings with a condition: longest without repeats, shortest summing to at least K, count of subarrays with product below K. The key question that tells you it applies: "if I move the left edge right, can the window flip from valid back to invalid in a way I cannot recover from?" If the condition is monotonic (shrinking a valid window keeps it valid, or shrinking an invalid window is the only repair), the window works.

Recognition signal

  • "Longest / shortest / count of contiguous subarray or substring."
  • The condition involves frequencies, sums, or products over the slice.
  • Brute force would be "try every start, extend every end" (O(n squared)).

The template

# Variable-size window: longest/shortest satisfying a condition
from collections import Counter
l = 0
window = Counter()
best = 0
for r, x in enumerate(s):          # r only moves forward
    window[x] += 1                 # grow
    while not valid(window):       # shrink until valid again
        window[s[l]] -= 1
        l += 1                     # l only moves forward
    best = max(best, r - l + 1)

# Fixed-size window: slide and update in O(1)
window_sum = sum(nums[:k])
best = window_sum
for r in range(k, len(nums)):
    window_sum += nums[r] - nums[r - k]
    best = max(best, window_sum)

Complexity

O(n) time, O(k) space where k is the alphabet or distinct-element count in the window. The time argument that matters: each pointer moves at most n steps, so the inner while runs at most n times total across the whole loop, not n times per iteration. Amortized O(1) per step (amortized: the average cost per step over the whole run, even though some single steps cost more).

Traced examples

Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (#3). s = "abcabcbb". 
r=0 a: window{a}            valid, best=1
r=1 b: window{a,b}          valid, best=2
r=2 c: window{a,b,c}        valid, best=3
r=3 a: window{a:2,b,c}      INVALID -> shrink: drop s[0]=a, l=1. window{a,b,c} valid, len 3
r=4 b: window{a,b:2,c}      INVALID -> drop s[1]=b, l=2. valid, len 3
r=5 c: window{a,b,c:2}      INVALID -> drop s[2]=c, l=3. valid, len 3
r=6 b: window{a:1,b:2,c:1}  INVALID -> drop s[3]=a, l=4; drop s[4]=b, l=5. valid "cb", len 2
r=7 b: window{c:1,b:2}      INVALID -> drop s[5]=c, l=6; drop s[6]=b, l=7. valid "b", len 1
answer = 3

The subtle point: shrinking removes from the left in order, which is exactly right because the duplicate's earlier copy is always the leftmost offender. Using a last-seen index map lets you jump l directly, but the map version has its own trap: only move l forward (l = max(l, last[x] + 1)), never backward.

Minimum Window Substring (#76). s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC".

Need counts of A, B, C covered. Expand r; when all needs are met, shrink l as far as possible while still covered, recording the best window.

need = {A:1, B:1, C:1}; have counts rise as r advances
r=5 (E): window has A,D,O,B,E -> A:1,B:1,C:0. not covered
r=6 (C): C:1 -> COVERED. shrink l:
  drop A(0): A:0 -> uncovered. stop. window = s[1..6] = "DOBECODE", len 6. best=6
r=9 (B): B:2, covered. shrink: drop D,O,B,E,C,O -> l=8? work it: window s[8..9]="EB" no...
  (trace continues; the second covered window found is "BANC", len 4)
answer = "BANC"

Common misunderstanding: the shrink loop must check coverage after every single left move, and "covered" needs a counter of satisfied distinct characters, not a re-scan of the need map (that would be O(alphabet) per step; the counter keeps it O(1)).

Sliding Window Maximum (#239). nums = [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3.

A decreasing deque (double-ended queue) of indices holds candidates: front is the current max. New element evicts smaller values from the back; indices outside the window fall off the front.

r=0 (1):   dq=[0]
r=1 (3):   pop 0 (1<3). dq=[1]
r=2 (-1):  dq=[1,2].            window [0..2], max=nums[1]=3
r=3 (-3):  dq=[1,2,3].          window [1..3], max=3
r=4 (5):   pop 3,2,1 (all <5). dq=[4]. window [2..4], max=5
r=5 (3):   dq=[4,5].            window [3..5], max=5
r=6 (6):   pop 5,4. dq=[6].     window [4..6], max=6
r=7 (7):   pop 6. dq=[7].       window [5..7], max=7
answer = [3,3,5,5,6,7]

Why decreasing? The deque always lists candidates from largest to smallest, so the max is at the front in O(1). Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(n) total. The trap is storing values instead of indices: you cannot tell when a value left the window.

Common traps

  • Non-monotonic conditions. "Subarray sum exactly K with negative numbers" breaks the basic window (shrinking can raise the sum back above K); that is a prefix-sum hash map problem (#560), not a window problem.
  • Moving l backward in the last-seen-index optimization.
  • Values instead of indices in the deque for #239.
  • Recomputing validity from scratch each step instead of maintaining counts incrementally.
"For contiguous slices with a monotone condition, I grow the right edge and shrink the left only until the condition holds again: both edges move forward, so the whole scan is linear."

#643Maximum Average Subarray IEasyFixed-size window sum.Atlas: full treatment
#209Minimum Size Subarray SumMediumVariable window: shrink while sum is enough.Atlas: full treatment
#3 MUST-DOLongest Substring Without Repeating CharactersMediumWindow plus last-seen index map.Atlas: full treatment

Key takeaways

  • Monotonicity is the admission ticket; without it, use prefix sums.
  • Maintain window state incrementally; never re-scan.
  • Interview relevance: the interviewer listens for the "each element enters and leaves once" argument and for you naming when the pattern fails.

Lab

Implement #3 twice: with the inner while-shrink and with the last-seen jump. Feed both a 10^6-character random string and compare times. Then break the window deliberately on an array with negatives and "sum exactly K" to feel the monotonicity requirement fail.

Next: Pattern 4 looks backward instead of forward: stacks remember what you have seen, in order.

4. Stacks and Monotonic Stacks

Windows scan forward. Some problems need to look backward at what you have already seen, in order. That is a stack.

On the board

"Match every opening bracket with its closer. What data structure remembers the most recent unmatched opener?" Then: "For each position, find the next greater element. Why is the naive scan O(n squared), and how does a stack make it O(n)?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The staircase. Stack contents stay in decreasing order from bottom to top; that invariant is the whole data structure.
  2. The incoming bar (new). Before it can be pushed, every smaller bar on top must pop.
  3. The faded poppers. Each popped bar just learned its next greater element: the incoming bar. One pop per element, ever.
  4. What breaks. If the order is not maintained (equal elements handled inconsistently), the "next greater" answers shift by one position. Decide strict vs non-strict up front.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Arrays (Ch 1). New here: last-in-first-out order and the monotonic invariant.

A stack is a last-in-first-out pile: you push items on top and pop from the top. It is the data structure for recency: "the most recent unmatched thing is the one I need." Parentheses matching, undo history, and nested structures all run on stacks.

A monotonic stack adds one rule: the stack always stays sorted (increasing or decreasing). When a new element arrives, you pop everything that violates the order. The elements you pop have just met the first element that beats them, which answers "next greater / smaller element" for every position in a single pass. This pattern exists because "for each position, scan forward until you find a bigger one" is O(n squared), and the stack turns it into O(n): each element is pushed once and popped once.

Recognition signal

  • "Valid / balanced / nested" (plain stack).
  • "Next greater / smaller element", "for each position find the nearest bigger", "daily temperatures".
  • "Largest rectangle", "trapping rain water" (monotonic stack variant).
  • The answer for position i depends on the first element to its left or right with some property.

The template

# Plain stack: matching / nesting
stack = []
for c in s:
    if c in "([{":
        stack.append(c)
    else:
        if not stack or not matches(stack.pop(), c):
            return False
return not stack

# Monotonic stack: next greater element (stores indices, decreasing values)
ans = [-1] * len(nums)
stack = []
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:   # x is the next greater for all of these
        j = stack.pop()
        ans[j] = i                            # (or i - j for distance)
    stack.append(i)

Complexity

O(n) time, O(n) space. The while loop looks nested, but each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so total pops are at most n. Space is the stack in the worst case (strictly decreasing input keeps everything).

Traced examples

Daily Temperatures (#739). temps = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73].

For each day, how many days until a warmer one? Decreasing stack of indices.

i=0 (73): stack empty -> push.            stack=[0]
i=1 (74): pop 0 (73<74): ans[0]=1. push.  stack=[1]
i=2 (75): pop 1 (74<75): ans[1]=1. push.  stack=[2]
i=3 (71): 75>71, push.                    stack=[2,3]
i=4 (69): push.                            stack=[2,3,4]
i=5 (72): pop 4 (69<72): ans[4]=1; pop 3 (71<72): ans[3]=2; 75>72 stop. push. stack=[2,5]
i=6 (76): pop 5 (72<76): ans[5]=1; pop 2 (75<76): ans[2]=4; push. stack=[6]
i=7 (73): 76>73, push.                    stack=[6,7]
answer = [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0]

Notice the invariant: after processing i, the stack holds indices with strictly decreasing temperatures, all waiting for their warmer day. The day that pops them is exactly the first warmer day because any earlier warmer day would have popped them already.

Largest Rectangle in Histogram (#84). heights = [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3].

For each bar, the rectangle it anchors extends left and right until a shorter bar. An increasing stack finds, for each popped bar, the first shorter bar on the right (the popper) and the first shorter on the left (the new top). Width = right - left - 1.

Append sentinel 0. Increasing stack of indices.
i=0 (2): push [0]
i=1 (1): pop 0: height 2, left = -1 (stack empty), right = 1. width=1-(-1)-1=1. area=2. push [1]
i=2 (5): push [1,2]
i=3 (6): push [1,2,3]
i=4 (2): pop 3: h=6, left=2, right=4. width=4-2-1=1. area=6.
         pop 2: h=5, left=1, right=4. width=4-1-1=2. area=10. <- best so far
         push [1,4]
i=5 (3): push [1,4,5]
i=6 (0): pop 5: h=3, left=4, right=6. width=1. area=3.
         pop 4: h=2, left=1, right=6. width=4. area=8.
         pop 1: h=1, left=-1, right=6. width=6. area=6.
answer = 10

The common misunderstanding: the width formula. When bar j pops, the popper i is the first index right of j with a smaller height, and the new stack top is the first index left of j with a smaller height. Everything strictly between them is at least as tall, so the anchored width is exactly i - left - 1. Draw it once and the formula becomes obvious.

Valid Parentheses (#20). s = "{[()]}". 
c='{': push.            stack=['{']
c='[': push.            stack=['{','[']
c='(': push.            stack=['{','[','(']
c=')': pop '(' matches. stack=['{','[']
c=']': pop '[' matches. stack=['{']
c='}': pop '{' matches. stack=[]
stack empty -> True

The two failure modes: a closer with an empty stack (extra closer), and a non-empty stack at the end (unclosed opener). Checking both is the whole problem; the mismatch check in the middle is just bookkeeping.

Common traps

  • Strict vs non-strict comparisons. Use < for "next greater", <= for "next greater or equal". Mixing them shifts answers by one. State the choice before coding.
  • Forgetting the sentinel in #84: leftover bars in the stack never get evaluated. Append a 0-height bar (or flush the stack in a final loop).
  • Storing values instead of indices when the answer needs positions or distances.
  • Circular arrays (#503): iterate 2n indices with i % n, but push each index only during the first pass.
"A stack remembers the most recent unmatched item; a monotonic stack keeps the waiting items sorted so the first element that beats them settles all of them at once, in linear time."

Key takeaways

  • Plain stack: recency and nesting. Monotonic stack: "first element to the left/right with property X", one pass.
  • Each element pushes once and pops once: that is the O(n) proof.
  • Interview relevance: monotonic stack is a known hard-pattern signal. Deriving it from the "scan forward" brute force, rather than reciting it, is what separates memorization from understanding.

Lab

Solve #739, then change the comparison from < to <= and diff the answers on an input with equal adjacent temperatures. Then implement #84 with and without the sentinel (a dummy boundary value that removes edge-case checks) and verify both give the same answer.

Next: Pattern 5 exploits order to discard half the search space per step: binary search.

5. Binary Search (including Binary Search on Answer)

Stacks exploit recency. Binary search exploits order: each comparison discards half of the remaining search space.

On the board

"Find the minimum eating speed so she finishes in h hours. The array is not sorted; where is the binary search?" Then: "Write the loop so it cannot infinite-loop. What is your invariant?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The sorted array. Values rise left to right; mid is highlighted coral.
  2. The discarded half (dimmed, X). The comparison at mid proved the answer is not there. This is the information half of the work.
  3. The kept half (teal). The new search space. It is at most half the old one, hence O(log n).
  4. What breaks. If the predicate is not monotonic (the kept half could still be wrong), binary search silently returns a wrong answer. Monotonicity is the contract.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Sorted arrays (Ch 1) and Big-O (Figure 2). New here: the halving argument and the monotonic predicate.

Binary search finds a boundary in a sorted space by halving it: check the middle, discard the half that cannot contain the answer, repeat. n becomes n/2, n/4, ... so it takes O(log n) steps.

The deeper version, binary search on answer, applies the same halving to a number you are choosing, not finding. The trick: define a yes/no question feasible(x) ("can I finish at speed x?") that is monotonic: false, false, ..., false, true, true, ..., true. Then binary-search the smallest x with a true answer. The array is gone; the search space is a range of candidate answers. Problems like Koko Eating Bananas (#875), Ship Packages (#1011), and Split Array are all the same machine with different predicates.

Recognition signal

  • "Sorted array" plus "find / insert position / first / last".
  • "Minimize the maximum" or "maximize the minimum" (classic binary-search-on-answer phrasing).
  • "K workers / h hours / d days" with a monotonic feasibility check.
  • You can write feasible(x) easily but cannot compute the answer directly.

The template

# Leftmost True of a monotonic predicate. Invariant: answer in [lo, hi].
def feasible(mid): ...   # False...False, True...True

lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
ans = hi
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if feasible(mid):
        ans = mid
        hi = mid - 1     # answer could be smaller; keep searching left
    else:
        lo = mid + 1     # mid is impossible; discard it
return ans

Complexity

O(log n) iterations times the cost of feasible. The classic trap is a predicate that costs O(n), making the total O(n log n), which is still usually fine. The invariant that prevents infinite loops: hi - lo strictly shrinks every iteration because mid is always excluded from the new range.

Traced examples

Koko Eating Bananas (#875). piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8.

Feasible(k): hours = sum of ceil(pile / k); return hours <= 8. Monotonic: faster never needs more hours. Search k in [1, 11].

lo=1, hi=11
mid=6:  hours = 1+1+2+2 = 6 <= 8 -> True.  ans=6, hi=5
mid=3:  hours = 1+2+3+4 = 10 > 8  -> False. lo=4
mid=4:  hours = 1+2+2+3 = 8  <= 8 -> True.  ans=4, hi=3
lo=4 > hi=3: stop.
answer = 4

Design notes that matter: the lower bound is 1, not 0 (division by zero); the upper bound is max(piles) (faster than the biggest pile is never needed). Ceil division without floats: (p + k - 1) // k.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array (#33). nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0.

The array is two sorted halves. At any mid, one half is guaranteed sorted; check whether the target lies in the sorted half's range.

lo=0, hi=6, mid=3 (7): left half [4..7] sorted. target 0 in [4,7]? no -> lo=4
lo=4, hi=6, mid=5 (1): left half [0..1] sorted. target 0 in [0,1]? yes -> hi=4
lo=4, hi=4, mid=4 (0): found.
answer = 4

The trap: comparing nums[mid] with nums[lo] (not nums[hi]) to identify the sorted half. And with duplicates (#81, not in the ladder), the sorted-half test can tie, which is why duplicates need the extra shrink step.

Median of Two Sorted Arrays (#4). A = [1, 3], B = [2].

Binary-search the split point i in the shorter array: take i from A and j = half - i from B so the left parts hold half the elements. Correct when A[i-1] <= B[j] and B[j-1] <= A[i]; then the median is max of left parts (and min of right parts for even length).

A=[1,3] (m=2), B=[2] (n=1). total=3, half=2.
lo=0, hi=2. mid i=1: j=2-1=1.
  A left=[1], B left=[2]. Check 1 <= B[1]? B[1] out of range = +inf. ok.
  Check B[0]=2 <= A[1]=3? yes. Correct split.
  median = max(1, 2) = 2 (odd length).
answer = 2.0

This is the famous hard problem, and the pattern is pure binary search on a partition index. The common misunderstanding is that you binary-search a value; you binary-search the split position, and the feasibility condition is the cross-inequality. Edge handling with -inf/+inf sentinels for empty sides is the implementation detail that sinks most attempts.

Common traps

  • Infinite loop: always exclude mid from the next range (mid - 1 / mid + 1), and use lo <= hi with the exclusion, or lo < hi with careful mid bias.
  • Non-monotonic predicate: verify false...false,true...true before coding. If feasibility can flip back, binary search is wrong, not slow.
  • Bounds: 0 vs 1 lower bound; inclusive vs exclusive upper bound. Write them from the predicate's domain, not from memory.
  • Overflow in other languages: mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2. In Python it does not matter, but interviewers ask.
"Binary search finds the boundary where a yes-or-no question flips from false to true; on sorted arrays the question is about position, on answer-spaces the question is feasibility, and the template never changes."

  • Interview relevance: "binary search on answer" is the L5+ signal. Say "minimize the maximum" out loud when you spot it.

Lab

Implement the leftmost-true template once, then solve #875, #1011, and #1482 by only writing new feasible functions and bounds. Time how little the loop code changes: that is the point.

Next: Pattern 6 trades away random access: linked lists, cheap splicing, and pointers meeting pointers.

6. Linked Lists

Arrays give random access. Linked lists give the opposite trade: no indices, but cheap splicing anywhere. The pointer skills from the foundations chapter finally meet a structure built from pointers.

On the board

"Reverse this list in place. Where do you keep your place while rewiring?" Then: "Detect a cycle without extra memory." Then: "Why does the fast pointer move twice as fast, and what does the meeting point prove?"

How to read this diagram

  1. Boxes and next arrows. Each node holds a value and one outgoing arrow. No indexing exists; you can only follow arrows.
  2. The curved teal arrows. The rewiring: curr.next = prev flips each arrow to point backward, one node per step.
  3. prev. The already-reversed prefix. Without it, flipping the first arrow orphans the rest of the list.
  4. What breaks. Forgetting to save nxt = curr.next before flipping loses the unprocessed suffix forever.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Recursion (Foundations). New here: rewiring pointers without losing your place.

A linked list is a chain of nodes; each node stores a value and a pointer (next) to the following node. Unlike an array, there is no index: reaching the k-th node costs k steps. The payoff is O(1) insertion and deletion once you hold the neighboring nodes.

Linked-list problems punish two things: losing your place while rewiring, and special-casing the head. Three tools fix both. A dummy head (a fake node before the real head) makes every insertion and deletion uniform, including at position 0. Fast/slow pointers (one moves two steps, one moves one) detect cycles and find middles in one pass. In-place reversal with a prev pointer is the primitive that reorder, palindrome-check, and k-group problems are built from.

Recognition signal

  • "Linked list" plus "reverse / merge / reorder / cycle / middle / remove nth from end."
  • "In place" with "one pass" (fast/slow).
  • "Deep copy" with extra pointers (interleave trick).

The template

class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

# Dummy head: every insertion/deletion looks the same
dummy = ListNode(0, head)
prev = dummy
# ... rewire prev.next freely; answer is dummy.next

# In-place reversal
prev, curr = None, head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next     # 1. save the rest of the list
    curr.next = prev    # 2. flip this arrow
    prev, curr = curr, nxt   # 3. advance both

# Fast and slow: cycle detection, middle finding
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
# fast reached the end -> slow is at the middle; meeting -> cycle

Complexity

O(n) time, O(1) space for nearly the whole chapter. That is the point of the pattern: linked lists are where you prove you can do real work without auxiliary arrays. Recursive solutions are O(n) stack space; know both and state the trade.

Traced examples

Reverse Linked List (#206). 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> None. 
prev=None, curr=1
step1: nxt=2; 1.next=None; prev=1, curr=2     None <- 1   2 -> 3
step2: nxt=3; 2.next=1;   prev=2, curr=3     None <- 1 <- 2   3
step3: nxt=None; 3.next=2; prev=3, curr=None  None <- 1 <- 2 <- 3
return prev (3)

Draw the boxes before coding; the most common bug is advancing curr before saving nxt. A useful invariant to state: after each step, prev heads the fully reversed prefix and curr heads the untouched suffix.

Reorder List (#143). 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 becomes 1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3.

Three primitives composed: (1) fast/slow finds the middle (3); (2) reverse the second half: 5 -> 4 -> 3; (3) interleave the halves.

halves:  1 -> 2 -> 3        and        5 -> 4 -> 3 (reversed second half)
merge:   1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3 -> None
(take from first, then second, alternating; the shared node 3 ends the list)

The trap: the middle node belongs to both halves conceptually; split the list explicitly (slow.next = None) before reversing, or the interleave loops forever.

Copy List with Random Pointer (#138). Each node has next and random.

The interleave trick avoids the hash map: (1) weave copy nodes in: A -> A' -> B -> B'; (2) set X'.random = X.random.next (the copy of any node sits right after the original); (3) unweave into two lists.

original:  A --random--> C
weave:     A -> A' -&> B -> B' -> C -> C'
fix:       A'.random = A.random.next = C'     (one hop lands on the copy)
unweave:   restore A->B->C and extract A'->B'->C'

Why it matters: it is the canonical "O(1) space with a clever invariant" answer. The common misunderstanding is that the hash map version is "wrong"; it is correct and simpler, O(n) space. State both, then offer the interleave as the space optimization.

Common traps

  • Losing the list: always save next before rewiring.
  • Head special cases: use a dummy head; never branch on "is this the first node".
  • Cycle II (#142): after slow/fast meet, reset one pointer to head and walk both at speed 1; they meet at the cycle entry. Know the phase argument (distance head-to-entry equals distance meeting-to-entry along the cycle).
  • None checks: while fast and fast.next, in that order.
"Linked lists reward pointer surgery: one extra pointer per operation, a dummy head so the head is never special, and fast/slow whenever one pass must do the work of two."

Key takeaways

  • Three tools cover the chapter: dummy head, in-place reversal, fast/slow.
  • Draw boxes and arrows before writing code; rewiring bugs are visual, not logical.
  • Interview relevance: linked lists test whether you can manipulate structure without an index crutch. Clean pointer discipline is the signal.

Lab

Implement #206 recursively and iteratively; measure stack depth on a 10^5-node list (the recursive version will hit Python's recursion limit: feel the O(n) stack space). Then implement #142 and verify the entry-finding walk on a hand-built cycle.

Next: Pattern 7 branches: trees, hierarchies, and traversals as the universal tool.

7. Trees and Traversals

Linked lists are chains. Trees are the first branching structure, and traversals are the universal tool for reading them.

On the board

"Solve it for the children, combine at the parent: which traversal is that?" Then: "Validate this BST. Why does checking each node against its parent fail?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The tree. Navy root, teal internal nodes, coral leaves: 7 nodes, each with at most two children.
  2. The dashed path with numbers 1 to 7. A traversal order: the sequence in which nodes are visited. Different orders (preorder, inorder, postorder, level order) trace different paths.
  3. What it teaches. The path is the algorithm's information flow: preorder carries decisions down, postorder carries results up, level order sweeps across.
  4. What breaks. Picking the wrong order means the information you need is not ready when you need it (e.g. computing a height in preorder, before the children's heights exist).

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Recursion (Foundations), stacks and queues (Ch 4). New here: traversals as information flow.

A tree is a hierarchy: one root, each node having zero or more children, with no cycles. A binary tree allows at most two children per node (left and right). A binary search tree (BST) adds an ordering rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, everything in the right is larger, which makes inorder traversal visit values in sorted order.

Trees are recursion's home turf, and almost every tree problem is one of four traversals wearing a costume:

  • Preorder (node, left, right): carry decisions down. Use for building, copying, serializing.
  • Inorder (left, node, right): visits a BST in sorted order. Use for validation and kth-smallest.
  • Postorder (left, right, node): children report up. Use for heights, diameters, path sums, anything "for every subtree".
  • Level order / BFS: sweep level by level with a queue. Use for anything "per level" or shortest-ish.

Recognition signal

  • "For every subtree / path / node, compute..." (postorder returning info upward).
  • "Level", "right side view", "zigzag" (BFS with per-level slices).
  • "BST" plus "validate / kth smallest / LCA" (inorder or the ordering property).
  • "Construct / serialize / flatten" (preorder plus structure).

The template

# Postorder DFS: children report up, combine at me
def dfs(node):
    if not node:
        return 0                    # base: define the empty-tree value
    left = dfs(node.left)
    right = dfs(node.right)
    return 1 + max(left, right)     # combine: the problem-specific line

# BFS level order with per-level slices
from collections import deque
q = deque([root])
while q:
    level = []
    for _ in range(len(q)):         # freeze the level size first
        node = q.popleft()
        level.append(node.val)
        if node.left: q.append(node.left)
        if node.right: q.append(node.right)
    process(level)

# BST validation with bounds carried down
def valid(node, lo, hi):
    return (not node
            or (lo < node.val < hi
                and valid(node.left, lo, node.val)
                and valid(node.right, node.val, hi)))

Complexity

O(n) time (each node visited once), O(h) stack space where h is the height: O(log n) for balanced trees, O(n) for a degenerate chain. BFS is O(n) time and O(w) space where w is the max width. State both; interviewers ask.

Traced examples

Diameter of Binary Tree (#543). Tree: 1 with left 2 (children 4, 5) and right 3.

Diameter = longest path between any two nodes = for some node, left height + right height. Postorder computes heights bottom-up; a global (or returned) best tracks the max sum.

        1
       / \
      2   3
     / \
    4   5
dfs(4)=1, dfs(5)=1 -> at 2: best = max(best, 1+1)=2; return 1+max(1,1)=2
dfs(3)=1 -> at 1: best = max(2, 2+1)=3; return 3
answer = 3  (path 4-2-5 is length 2 edges; 4-2-1-3 is 3)

The trap: returning the diameter from dfs instead of the height. The recursion must return what the parent needs (height); the answer is side-channel state. Mixing the two is the classic bug.

Validate Binary Search Tree (#98). Tree: root 5, left 4 (left 3), right 6.

Each node must satisfy lo < val < hi with bounds tightened by ancestors. Checking only the parent fails on grandchild violations (a classic: root 5, left 10 is caught, but root 5, left 3 with right child 6 is missed by parent-only checks).

valid(5, -inf, +inf):  ok. left valid(4, -inf, 5), right valid(6, 5, +inf)
valid(4, -inf, 5): ok. left valid(3, -inf, 4): ok, leaf.
valid(6, 5, +inf): ok, leaf.
-> True
counter-example for parent-only check:
    5
   /
  3
   \
    6     <- 6 > 5 violates BST, but 6 > 3 passes a parent-only check

Common misunderstanding: "inorder gives sorted order, so just check the inorder list is sorted" is also correct and simpler to write, but it is O(n) extra space unless done iteratively with a previous-value variable. Know both; the bounds version is O(h) space.

Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (#124). Tree: root -10, left 9, right 20 (children 15, 7).

Like diameter, but the path value is a sum and nodes can be negative. dfs returns the best downward path starting at the node (clamped at 0: a negative branch is dropped); the global best considers paths passing through the node (left + node + right).

dfs(9)=9; dfs(15)=15; dfs(7)=7
at 20: through = 15+20+7 = 42 -> best=42; return 20+max(15,7)=35
at -10: through = 9 + (-10) + 35 = 34; best stays 42; return -10+max(9,35,0)=25
answer = 42  (path 15-20-7)

The trap: returning the through-path upward. The parent can only extend a path that goes down through one side, so dfs returns val + max(0, left, right), never the sum of both sides.

Common traps

  • Wrong traversal order for the information flow (height in preorder).
  • Returning the answer instead of the subproblem value in postorder (#543, #124).
  • BST validation against parent only instead of ancestor bounds.
  • BFS level slicing: capture len(q) before the inner loop; the queue grows as you drain it.
  • Recursion depth: a skewed tree recurses n deep; Python's default limit is 1000.
"Trees are recursion with a direction: preorder carries decisions down, postorder carries answers up, inorder reads a BST in order, and level order sweeps across; I pick the traversal whose information flow matches the question."

Key takeaways

  • Four traversals, four information flows. Name the flow before coding.
  • Postorder: return what the parent needs, track the answer on the side.
  • Interview relevance: tree problems are the cleanest test of recursive thinking. A strong candidate states the traversal choice and its reason in one sentence.

Lab

Implement all four traversals iteratively (explicit stack for the DFS ones) on the same tree and verify the orders. Then break #98's bounds version by replacing ancestor bounds with parent checks and find the smallest failing tree.

Next: Pattern 8 specializes trees for strings: tries, where prefixes are paths.

8. Tries

Trees branch by value. Tries are trees specialized for strings: every prefix is a path, and a million prefix queries stop being expensive.

On the board

"A million words, a million prefix queries. A hash set answers 'is this a word' but not 'which words start with pre'. What structure shares the work across queries?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The root. The empty prefix; every word starts here.
  2. Letter edges. Each edge adds one character. Following edges spells the prefix.
  3. Shared navy path. Words with a common prefix share nodes: the storage and the search work are shared too.
  4. Word flags (teal). A node can be both a prefix of longer words and a complete word; the flag distinguishes.
  5. What breaks. Without the flag, "app" would be indistinguishable from the prefix of "apple". The flag is the data, not decoration.

How to read this diagram

  1. Levels are bit positions. Bit 2 (the 4s) is decided at the top edge, bit 1 (the 2s) in the middle, bit 0 (the 1s) at the leaves. 4 = 100, 5 = 101, 6 = 110.
  2. Shared prefixes share nodes. 4 and 5 share the path 1-0 and split only at the last bit. The trie never stores a prefix twice.
  3. The amber path is a max-XOR query. For x = 1 (001), at each bit prefer the child holding the opposite bit: bit 2 wants 0 (absent, take 1), bit 1 wants 1 (take it), bit 0 wants 0 (take it). The path 1-1-0 reaches 6, and 6 ^ 1 = 7, the largest XOR with 1 among the stored numbers.
  4. What breaks. A binary trie answers max-XOR in O(bits) time, but for plain existence checks it is just an expensive hash set. The win is only for bitwise queries.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Trees (Ch 7), hash sets (Ch 1). New here: edges as letters, plus the binary trie for XOR.

A trie (prefix tree, pronounced "try") is a tree where each edge is a letter and each root-to-node path spells a prefix. Inserting and searching a word costs O(word length), independent of how many words are stored. A hash set can tell you whether a word exists, but it cannot enumerate "all words starting with pre" without scanning everything; a trie walks to the pre node and reads off the subtree.

This pattern exists for prefix-heavy workloads: autocomplete, spell checking, word games on boards, and XOR problems (XOR, written ^, outputs 1 exactly where two bits differ; a binary trie stores numbers bit by bit). The recognition cue is a dictionary plus many queries about prefixes or shared structure.

Recognition signal

  • "Given a dictionary of words" plus "prefix / autocomplete / search with wildcards".
  • Word Search on a grid with many words (trie prunes dead branches).
  • "Maximum XOR pair" (binary trie: the same structure over bits).
  • Many queries sharing prefixes; a hash set would repeat work per query.

The template

class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}   # char -> TrieNode (array of 26 is faster in hot loops)
        self.is_word = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for c in word:
            node = node.children.setdefault(c, TrieNode())
        node.is_word = True   # the flag: prefix vs complete word

    def search(self, word):
        node = self._walk(word)
        return node is not None and node.is_word

    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None

    def _walk(self, s):
        node = self.root
        for c in s:
            node = node.children.get(c)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

Complexity

O(L) per insert/search where L is word length; space O(total characters). A wildcard search (#211, where '.' matches any single letter) can fan out: worst case O(26^L) in theory, fine in practice with pruning (cutting off search branches that cannot lead to an answer). State the trade: a trie beats a hash set only when queries exploit shared prefixes; for pure exact lookups it is just a heavier set.

Traced examples

Implement Trie (#208). insert("apple"), search("apple"), search("app"), startsWith("app"). 
insert apple: root-a-p-p-l-e, flag at e
search apple: walk a-p-p-l-e -> node exists, is_word True -> True
search app:   walk a-p-p -> node exists, is_word False -> False
startsWith app: walk a-p-p -> node exists -> True

The entire problem is the flag. Forgetting is_word makes search and startsWith identical, which fails the second assertion above.

Word Search II (#212). Board with words ["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"].

Naive: run grid DFS per word; dead branches repeat across words sharing prefixes. Trie version: insert all words, then DFS the board once, walking the trie in parallel; when the trie walk dies, prune the whole branch (no word with this prefix exists).

trie has 'o'->'a'->'t'->'h' and 'e'->'a'->'t' sharing the 'a' node? (they share nothing but structure)
board DFS from 'o': trie walk o-a-t-h alive -> found "oath", mark is_word False (dedupe)
board DFS from 'p': trie has no 'p' child -> prune immediately, zero deeper work
The pruning is the speedup: each board path is explored only while some word needs it.

Two practical details: (1) clear is_word after finding a word to avoid duplicate reports; (2) optionally prune leaf nodes from the trie as words are found, which speeds up later searches. Both are common follow-up material.

Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (#421). nums = [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8].

Insert each number's 32-bit form into a binary trie. For each number, walk the trie greedily preferring the opposite bit at each position (1 where the number has 0): the greedy choice is safe because a higher differing bit always outweighs all lower bits combined.

nums in 5 bits: 3=00011, 10=01010, 5=00101, 25=11001, 2=00010, 8=01000
query 25 (11001): prefer 0,0,1,1,0 -> best partner 5? walk: bit4: prefer 0 -> exists (3,10,5,2,8 side)
  bit3: prefer 0 -> ...
  result 25^5 = 28? check: 25^5 = 28 (11001^00101=11100). best overall = 28 (25^5).
answer = 28

The misunderstanding to avoid: this is not "try all pairs". The trie makes each query O(32); total O(32n). The greedy bit choice works because XOR is lexicographic on bits from the top down.

Common traps

  • Missing the word flag (search vs startsWith collapse).
  • Wildcard DFS without pruning in #211: the . branch must try all children, which is correct but can blow up; mention it.
  • Rebuilding the trie per query instead of once per dictionary.
  • Memory: a dict-of-dicts trie is heavy; for lowercase English, a length-26 list per node is the standard optimization. State it when asked about scale.
"When many queries share prefixes, I store the dictionary as a trie: each query walks shared letter edges once, and the word flag separates complete words from mere prefixes."

Key takeaways

  • Trie = shared prefix work. O(L) operations independent of dictionary size.
  • The flag, the prune, and the greedy bit walk are the three ideas that recur.
  • Interview relevance: #212 is the classic hard that rewards the trie; #421 shows the structure generalizes beyond letters.

Lab

Benchmark: 100k random words, 10k prefix queries: trie vs hash set with manual prefix filtering. Measure where the trie wins and where the set is fine. Then implement #421 and verify the greedy choice against brute force on small inputs.

Next: Pattern 9 organizes by priority instead of prefix: heaps.

9. Heaps

Tries organize by prefix. Heaps organize by priority: the minimum or maximum is always on top, which is exactly what streaming problems need.

On the board

"Keep the k largest as a stream arrives. Sorting each time is O(n log n) per element; what is cheaper?" Then: "Median of a stream: one heap or two?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The tree. Max-heap: every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum sits at the root.
  2. The array below. The same tree stored flat: children of index i are at 2i+1, 2i+2. No pointers needed.
  3. The pop arrow. Removing the root takes the last element, puts it at the root, and sifts it down: O(log n).
  4. What breaks. A heap is not sorted; only the root is extreme. Scanning a heap for the k-th element without popping is O(n).

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Binary trees (Ch 7), arrays (Ch 1). New here: the heap order property and the array layout.

A heap (priority queue) is a structure that always hands you the most extreme element (smallest in a min-heap, largest in a max-heap) in O(1), with O(log n) insert and remove. It is a complete binary tree stored in an array; Python's heapq is a min-heap (negate values for max-heap behavior).

Heaps exist for running extremes: "k largest so far", "merge k sorted streams", "schedule with cooldowns". Whenever the question is "what is the most extreme thing right now, and it keeps changing", a heap beats re-sorting. The two signature moves: a size-k heap keeps a running shortlist (push everything, pop when bigger than k), and two heaps (a max-heap lower half and a min-heap upper half) maintain a running median.

Recognition signal

  • "K largest / smallest / closest / most frequent."
  • "Merge k sorted ..." (heap of current heads).
  • "Stream" plus "median / kth largest" (two heaps or size-k heap).
  • "Schedule / minimum refuels / furthest reachable" (greedy + heap for the best swap).

The template

import heapq

# Top-k: min-heap of size k holds the k largest
h = []
for x in nums:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
    if len(h) > k:
        heapq.heappop(h)          # evict the smallest of the shortlist
# h now holds the k largest; h[0] is the kth largest

# Running median: two balanced heaps
small = []   # max-heap via negatives: the lower half
large = []   # min-heap: the upper half
def add(x):
    heapq.heappush(small, -x)
    heapq.heappush(large, -heapq.heappop(small))  # move max of small over
    if len(large) > len(small):
        heapq.heappush(small, -heapq.heappop(large))  # rebalance
# median: -small[0] (odd count) or (-small[0] + large[0]) / 2

Complexity

O(n log k) for top-k over n elements; O(log n) per insertion for the median. Space O(k) / O(n). The comparison that matters: sorting is O(n log n) once, but on a stream you would re-sort per element; the heap pays only per update.

Traced examples

Kth Largest Element in an Array (#215). nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2. 
push 3: h=[3]
push 2: h=[2,3]
push 1: h=[1,2,3] -> len>2, pop 1 -> h=[2,3]
push 5: h=[2,3,5] -> pop 2 -> h=[3,5]
push 6: h=[3,5,6] -> pop 3 -> h=[5,6]
push 4: h=[4,5,6] -> pop 4 -> h=[5,6]
answer = h[0] = 5

The invariant: the heap always holds the k largest seen so far, so its minimum is the kth largest. The common alternative, quickselect, is O(n) average but O(n squared) worst case and mutates the array; name the trade.

Task Scheduler (#621). tasks = ["A","A","A","B","B","B"], n = 2.

Greedy: always run the task with the most remaining (max-heap on counts); between runs of the same task, n cooldown slots must pass. Simulate cycle by cycle, or compute directly: the answer is driven by the most frequent task.

counts: A:3, B:3. max-heap by remaining.
cycle 1: run A, B, idle   (A:2, B:2 left)
cycle 2: run A, B, idle   (A:1, B:1 left)
cycle 3: run A, B         (done)
answer = 8
formula check: (maxfreq-1)*(n+1) + numaxfreq = (3-1)*3 + 2 = 8

The formula version: the most frequent task's occurrences frame (maxfreq - 1) blocks of size n + 1, plus the tasks tying for max frequency in the last block. The trap: when tasks fill all idle slots, the answer is just len(tasks); take the max of the formula and the task count.

Merge k Sorted Lists (#23). lists = [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]].

Heap of current heads: pop the smallest, append it, push its successor. Each pop/push is O(log k); n total elements.

heap = [(1,l0),(1,l1),(2,l2)]
pop (1,l0) -> out [1], push (4,l0). heap=[(1,l1),(2,l2),(4,l0)]
pop (1,l1) -> out [1,1], push (3,l1). heap=[(2,l2),(3,l1),(4,l0)]
pop (2,l2) -> out [1,1,2], push (6,l2). ...
answer = [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]

Implementation trap in Python: tuples compare second elements on ties, and ListNodes are not comparable. Push (val, index, node) with a tiebreaker index, or wrap nodes.

Common traps

  • heapq is a min-heap. For max behavior, push negatives and remember to negate on the way out.
  • Tuple comparison on ties with unorderable payloads (#23).
  • Median rebalance invariant: len(small) >= len(large) and sizes differ by at most 1; every element of small is at most every element of large. Check both after each insert.
  • Re-sorting instead of heaping on streams; and the reverse mistake: using a heap for a one-shot top-k where nlargest or sort is clearer.
"For a running extreme I keep a heap, not a sorted list: a size-k min-heap holds the k largest, and two balanced heaps hold the median, each update costing a logarithm."

Key takeaways

  • Heap = extreme value under updates. Size-k shortlist and two-heap median are the two moves.
  • Negation gives max-heap behavior; tiebreakers prevent comparison crashes.
  • Interview relevance: heaps test whether you reach for the right structure for streaming extremes instead of re-sorting.

Lab

Feed 10^6 random ints through the size-k heap vs full sort for k = 10 and k = 10^5; find the k where sort wins. Then break the two-heap median by removing the rebalance step and watch the median drift on a sorted input.

Next: Pattern 10 orders by position on a line: intervals, merging, and sweeping.

10. Intervals

Heaps order by value. Intervals order by position on a line: meetings, ranges, and overlaps, where sorting by start makes the rest trivial.

On the board

"Merge all overlapping meetings. What is the first step, and why does it make the rest trivial?" Then: "Minimum rooms needed: why does sorting by start plus a heap of end times work?"

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: chaos. Unsorted intervals overlap arbitrarily; no local rule applies.
  2. The sort arrow. Sorting by start time lines everything up. This O(n log n) step is the price of admission.
  3. Right: the sweep. One left-to-right pass merges: if the next start is within the running end, extend; else start a new merged interval.
  4. What breaks. Sorting by end instead of start breaks merging (you lose the sweep order); sorting by end is for the greedy scheduling variant (#435). Know which sort each problem wants.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Sorting by a key, arrays (Ch 1). New here: the sweep line and the exchange argument.

An interval is a [start, end] pair: a meeting, a balloon, a task window. Interval problems look chaotic until you sort by start time: then the problem becomes a left-to-right sweep with three moves. Merge overlapping intervals into one. Detect overlap with the test max(starts) <= min(ends). Schedule greedily by sorting on end time and taking the earliest finisher first.

The pattern exists because time is one-dimensional: sorted by start, "does this overlap the running interval?" is a single comparison. The greedy scheduling variant works by an exchange argument: the earliest-finishing interval leaves the most room, so some optimal schedule includes it.

Recognition signal

  • "Merge / insert / remove overlaps", "meeting rooms", "minimum arrows".
  • "Maximum number of non-overlapping" (sort by end, greedy take).
  • "Minimum number of rooms / groups" (sweep with a heap of end times).
  • Input is pairs of [start, end] and the answer is about overlap or coverage.

The template

# Merge: sort by start, sweep
intervals.sort()                      # sorts by start, then end
merged = [intervals[0]]
for s, e in intervals[1:]:
    if s <= merged[-1][1]:            # overlaps the running interval
        merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], e)
    else:
        merged.append([s, e])

# Greedy scheduling: sort by END, take earliest finishers
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
count, end = 0, float('-inf')
for s, e in intervals:
    if s >= end:                      # no overlap with the last taken
        count += 1
        end = e

# Meeting rooms II: heap of end times
import heapq
intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
ends = []
for s, e in intervals:
    if ends and ends[0] <= s:
        heapq.heappop(ends)           # a room freed up
    heapq.heappush(ends, e)
rooms = len(ends)

Complexity

O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep; O(n) space worst case. Nearly every interval problem is sort-dominated; say so.

Traced examples

Merge Intervals (#56). [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. 
sorted (already): [1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]
merged=[[1,3]]
[2,6]:  2 <= 3 -> extend: merged=[[1,6]]
[8,10]: 8 > 6  -> new:    merged=[[1,6],[8,10]]
[15,18]: 15 > 10 -> new: merged=[[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]
answer = [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]

The overlap test uses the running merged end, not the previous interval's end: after extending to [1,6], the next comparison is against 6. Using the raw previous end is the standard bug on chains like [1,4],[2,3],[3,5].

Non-overlapping Intervals (#435). [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]].

Remove the fewest intervals to kill all overlaps = keep the most non-overlapping. Greedy: sort by end, keep an interval if its start is at or past the last kept end.

sort by end: [1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[3,4]
keep [1,2], end=2
[2,3]: 2 >= 2 keep, end=3
[1,3]: 1 < 3 skip (remove it)
[3,4]: 3 >= 3 keep, end=4
removed = 1

Why earliest-finish is safe (the exchange argument): consider any optimal solution; its first interval ends no earlier than our pick, so swapping in our pick cannot hurt feasibility and keeps the same count. Repeat. This is the justification interviewers want, not just the code.

Meeting Rooms II (#253). [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]. 
sort by start: [0,30],[5,10],[15,20]
[0,30]:  ends empty -> push 30.        ends=[30]
[5,10]:  ends[0]=30 > 5 -> no room free, push 10. ends=[10,30]
[15,20]: ends[0]=10 <= 15 -> pop 10 (room freed), push 20. ends=[20,30]
rooms = 2

The heap always holds the end times of meetings currently occupying rooms; its size is the rooms in use. The trap: popping only when ends[0] <= s (a meeting ending exactly when the next starts frees the room; < alone overcounts).

Common traps

  • Sorting by the wrong endpoint: merge/insert sort by start; greedy scheduling sorts by end.
  • Comparing against the raw previous interval instead of the running merged end.
  • Touching intervals: decide whether [1,2],[2,3] overlap per the problem statement (<= vs <); #435 uses >= (touching is fine), #56 merges on <=.
  • Insert Interval (#57): three phases: add non-overlapping-before, merge the overlapping run, add the rest. Do not re-sort after inserting; the input is already sorted.
"For intervals I sort first and ask which endpoint matters: start for merging and sweeping, end for greedy scheduling, and the sweep itself is always one linear pass."

Key takeaways

  • Sort by start to merge; sort by end to schedule; heap of ends to count rooms.
  • The exchange argument is the greedy justification; be ready to say it.
  • Interview relevance: interval problems are the canonical "sort plus sweep" test; the endpoint-choice question is the signal.

Lab

Solve #435 with sort-by-start instead of sort-by-end and find a failing case; this teaches why the endpoint matters. Then implement #57 in one pass without re-sorting.

Next: Pattern 11 handles what no shortcut covers: backtracking, systematic search with undo.

11. Backtracking

Every pattern so far had a clean structure: sorted input, a window, a heap. Backtracking is for the rest: systematic search with choose, explore, and undo.

On the board

"Generate all subsets. What is the recursive structure: what do you choose, and what do you undo?" Then: "Your output has duplicates. Where exactly do you skip, and why does sorting make it legal?"

How to read this diagram

  1. The tree. Each level is one decision (include element i or skip it). Root-to-leaf paths are candidate solutions.
  2. Choose (teal) / skip (coral). The two recursive branches at each level.
  3. Prune (gray X). A branch abandoned early because it cannot lead to a valid solution; this is where exponential search becomes practical.
  4. The star. A complete valid solution at a leaf.
  5. What breaks. Forgetting to unchoose corrupts the shared path for sibling branches; duplicates appear when equal choices are not skipped.

The pattern, from zero

Prerequisites. Recursion (Foundations), the DFS idea (Ch 7). New here: choose / explore / unchoose, and pruning.

Backtracking is depth-first search over decisions, not over graph nodes. The skeleton never changes: choose an option, explore recursively, unchoose (undo) to restore state for the next option. It exists for "generate / count all ..." problems: subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions, board placements. The search is exponential by nature; pruning (abandoning branches that cannot succeed) is what makes it finish.

The recognition cue is the word "all": all subsets, all permutations, all ways to parenthesize. If the problem asks for one answer, backtracking is usually overkill; if it asks for every answer, backtracking is usually the tool.

Recognition signal

  • "Generate all / list all / count all ..." (subsets, permutations, combinations).
  • Constraints are small (n at most ~20): the exponential is affordable.
  • "Place N queens", "solve the Sudoku", "partition into palindromes" (constraint propagation + DFS).
  • Duplicates in input with "unique" in the output (sort + skip rule).

The template

def backtrack(start, path):
    results.append(path[:])          # record a candidate (copy!)
    for i in range(start, len(nums)):
        if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]:
            continue                 # skip duplicate choices (needs sorted input)
        path.append(nums[i])         # CHOOSE
        backtrack(i + 1, path)       # EXPLORE
        path.pop()                   # UNCHOOSE: restore for the next sibling

# Permutation flavor: choose any unused slot
def permute(path, used):
    if len(path) == len(nums):
        results.append(path[:]); return
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        if used[i]: continue
        if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1] and not used[i-1]:
            continue                 # duplicate permutation skip rule
        used[i] = True
        path.append(nums[i])
        permute(path, used)
        path.pop(); used[i] = False   # unchoose both

Complexity

O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations, times O(n) copy cost per result. Space O(n) recursion depth plus the output. The honest statement: backtracking does not "optimize" the exponential away; pruning and small n make it viable. Say that.

Traced examples

Subsets (#78). nums = [1, 2, 3]. 
backtrack(0, []): record []
  i=0: choose 1 -> backtrack(1, [1]): record [1]
    i=1: choose 2 -> backtrack(2, [1,2]): record [1,2]
      i=2: choose 3 -> backtrack(3, [1,2,3]): record [1,2,3]; return
      unchoose 3
    unchoose 2
    i=2: choose 3 -> backtrack(3, [1,3]): record [1,3]; return
    unchoose 3
  unchoose 1
  i=1: choose 2 -> ... records [2], [2,3]
  i=2: choose 3 -> records [3]
results = [[],[1],[1,2],[1,2,3],[1,3],[2],[2,3],[3]]

The start index is what prevents [2,1] from appearing separately from [1,2]: each recursive call only considers later elements. The path[:] copy is not optional; without it every entry aliases the same mutating list.

Combination Sum (#39). candidates = [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7.

Unlimited reuse: the recursive call keeps the same index i (not i + 1), so 2 can be chosen repeatedly. Prune when the remainder goes negative.

bt(0, [], 7):
  choose 2 -> bt(0, [2], 5):
    choose 2 -> bt(0, [2,2], 3):
      choose 2 -> bt(0, [2,2,2], 1):
        choose 2 -> remainder -1: prune. unchoose
        choose 3 -> remainder -2: prune ...
        (6,7 prune immediately)
      unchoose 2; choose 3 -> bt(1, [2,2,3], 0): RECORD [2,2,3]
    ...
  choose 3 -> ... remainder 4: choose 3 -> 1, ... no
  choose 7 -> bt(3, [7], 0): RECORD [7]
answer = [[2,2,3],[7]]

The one-character difference from Combination Sum II (#40): recurse on i (reuse allowed) vs i + 1 (each used once). Interviewers love asking for both back to back; the delta is exactly this.

Word Search (#79). Board 3x4, word "ABCCED".

Grid DFS: from each cell matching the first letter, explore 4 neighbors for the next letter, marking visited by temporarily overwriting the cell (the unchoose step restores it).

board:                search "ABCCED" from (0,0)='A':
A B C E               (0,0) A ok -> mark '#'
S F C S               (0,1) B ok -> mark '#'
A D E E               (0,2) C ok -> (1,2) C ok -> (2,2) E ok -> (2,1) D ok
                      word consumed -> True (unwind, restoring cells)

The visited-marking trick (write '#', recurse, restore) avoids a separate visited set and is the standard in-grid implementation. The trap: restoring the cell on the way out even when the branch fails; forgetting it corrupts later searches from other start cells.

Common traps

  • Forgetting to unchoose: the shared path leaks choices into sibling branches.
  • Aliasing results: append path[:], never path.
  • Duplicate skip without sorting: the skip rules assume sorted input; sort first.
  • Reuse vs single-use: i vs i + 1 in the recursive call (#39 vs #40).
  • No pruning: check the bound (remainder, placement validity) before recursing, not after.
"Backtracking is choose, explore, unchoose on a decision tree; I prune dead branches early, copy the path into results, and sort plus skip whenever the input has duplicates."
